title: Superbad
full_review:
It is instructive, and indeed sobering to compare the comedy �Superbad� (Columbia) with one of its remote cinematic ancestors, 1973�s �American Grafitti.� Both films take place over the course of a single night and both trace the adventures of a group of high school friends who are about to graduate and go their separate ways.

The earlier movie, set in 1962, however, possesses an innocence and a sense of moral order completely alien to this jaded, chaotic world. . The films might as well be separated by several centuries, rather than by a mere 45 years.

�Superbad� focuses on the friendship between two nerdy high school seniors, Seth (Jonah Hill) and Evan (Michael Cera). Teaming up with their even more dweebish sidekick Fogell (Christopher Mintz-Plasse), they set off to pursue the girls of their dreams, Jules (Emma Stone), Becca (Martha MacIsaac) and Nichola (Aviva).

In order to gain admittance to a party with the girls, the friends must first purchase liquor using a fake ID. This brings them into contact with two comically immature policemen, Officers Slater (Bill Hader) and Michaels (Seth Rogan).

While Fogell goes off with the cops on a wild, increasingly drunken ride around town, Seth and Evan find themselves in the midst of an adult party too raucous even for their standards. The three eventually reunite and finally arrive at the party they are supposed to be attending, but the conclusion of the evening is not exactly what they�ve been expecting.

Director Greg Mottola�s film, written and produced by Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg, is unremittingly low-minded and vulgar, with hardly a line of dialogue that doesn�t contain an offensive word. There is a glimmer of morality in a few of the scenes, and the bond between the two main characters is shown to be stronger than any of the circumstances that challenge it. In the end, too, the main protagonists� plans of sexual conquest come to naught, and in the case of at least one, this is the result of a reasonably respectable moral choice.

If �Superbad� bears any relationship to real adolescent life, this is a bleak time to be growing up.
